title: Multi-Country P2P Rollout Strategy: How to Phase a Procure-to-Pay Implementation Across Southeast Asia
summary: Plan a phased P2P rollout across Southeast Asia: market sequencing, POC to approval, 12-16 week deployment cycles, UAT, cutover and adoption.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Rolling out procure-to-pay across five Southeast Asian countries works best in batches. Start with the markets that generate the most transactions relative to their complexity, not simply the largest headcount. Each batch runs a 12 to 16 week cycle: preparation, design, configuration, UAT, sign-off, role-based training, cutover dry run and go-live. Resolve ERP integration scope and approval design before configuration, and get the final approver into the proof of concept, because those two factors decide whether the timeline holds.


## Why Multi-Country P2P Rollouts Need a Different Plan


Rolling out P2P software in one office is a project. Rolling it out across Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam and Indonesia is a programme. Each market brings its own tax regime, language, supplier habits, approval culture and sometimes its own ERP configuration.


Peakflo recently worked through this planning with a regional finance team at a manufacturing and distribution group with five Southeast Asian subsidiaries. Their plan is a useful reference because it follows a pattern we see often:


- **Scope:** P2P first (purchase request to PO to invoice), with staff reimbursements and other requisitions in phase two because they are simpler
- **Volume:** a few hundred full P2P cycles a month across the region, with a few hundred users including requesters, approvers and finance
- **Sequencing:** Malaysia and Singapore first, representing roughly a quarter to a third of volume, even though Thailand has the most staff
- **Approval path:** a financial analyst runs discovery, the regional finance director joins for demo and pricing, and the APAC VP attends the POC and approves
- **Timeline:** project approval by year end, development and UAT in the first quarter, then go-live in the first markets


This guide turns that pattern into a repeatable rollout strategy. If you are earlier in your journey, our[procure-to-pay automation guide](https://peakflo.co/blog/procure-to-pay-automation-complete-guide) covers the fundamentals.


## Step 1: Define Phase 1 Scope Narrowly


The temptation is to automate everything at once. Resist it. The team above prioritised P2P because it was the most complicated process they had and the most important for controlling expense approvals and governance. Staff reimbursements were deferred because they are more straightforward and can be added quickly once the platform is in place.


A good phase 1 scope:


- Covers the process with the highest control risk
- Uses a small number of modules, for example PR creation, invoice capture, approval automation, PO matching and non-PO GL coding
- Leaves simpler processes, such as[expense management](https://peakflo.co/business-travel-and-expense-management) , for a fast second phase


## Step 2: Settle the ERP Integration Scope Before Anything Else


The single biggest cause of delay in regional P2P projects is an undecided integration scope. Will the P2P platform post only invoices to the ERP, or approved POs and goods receipts too? That decision changes data mapping, testing and effort.


In the discovery above, the integration scope with Oracle Fusion Cloud was flagged as the real blocker, because it decides the technical fitting agenda and implementation sizing. Our guide on[Oracle Fusion Cloud invoice-only integration](https://peakflo.co/blog/oracle-fusion-cloud-p2p-automation-invoice-only-integration) explains the options in detail.


## Step 3: Sequence Markets into Batches


Choosing which markets go first matters more than most teams expect. Headcount is a poor guide. Use these criteria instead:


Criterion Why it matters Example signal


Transaction volume High-volume markets prove the design under load and show savings early Most invoice and payment requests


Process maturity Documented processes configure faster Clear approval rules, clean supplier master


Language and tax similarity Similar markets can share one batch Shared English usage, comparable tax setup


Stakeholder availability UAT needs local key users Country finance lead committed


Business risk Avoid going live during peak season Quiet quarter for that market


The team in our example initially assumed Thailand would have the highest transaction volume because it had the most staff. Their investigation showed more invoice and payment requests came from Malaysia and Singapore. Those two markets also share English as a working language and have similar processes, so batching them together was a natural first step.


A typical five-country sequence might look like this:


Batch Markets Rationale Indicative timing


1 Malaysia and Singapore High transaction volume, English working language, similar processes First 12 to 16 week cycle


2 Thailand Largest user base, needs Thai interface and strong training Second cycle


3 Vietnam and Indonesia Smaller scale, distinct tax and e-invoicing needs Third cycle


## Step 4: Run a Proof of Concept with the Final Approver


Regional P2P projects are usually approved above the finance team running them. If the approver only sees slides, approval drags. If they sit in a POC that processes their own documents, the decision is usually quick.


A strong POC includes:


- Real purchase requests and POs from the first batch
- Real supplier invoices, including local-language and handwritten ones
- Approval routing that mirrors your actual matrix
- Matching against POs and receipts, plus non-PO GL coding
- Tax handling for each entity
- A test posting to the ERP


For a structured way to evaluate pilots, see our[90-day POC evaluation framework](https://peakflo.co/blog/90-day-poc-invoice-delivery-automation-evaluation-framework) .


## Step 5: Design and Configure Each Batch


Each deployment cycle follows the same stages. For a mid-market group, a cycle typically takes 12 to 16 weeks.


Stage Key activities Typical duration


Preparation Kick-off, data collection, stakeholder mapping 1 to 2 weeks


Design Approval matrix, roles, integration mapping, tax scenarios 2 to 3 weeks


Configuration Roles, policies, master data sync, templates, integrations 3 to 4 weeks


User acceptance testing Real scenarios per entity, defect fixes 2 to 3 weeks


Sign-off and training Formal sign-off, role-based training in local languages 1 to 2 weeks


Cutover dry run and go-live Rehearsal, open item load, go-live, hypercare 1 to 2 weeks


Design decisions made in batch 1, such as role names, approval group structure and tax code mapping, become templates for later batches. That is why later batches often run faster. Our guide to[approval matrix setup for multi-entity P2P](https://peakflo.co/blog/approval-matrix-setup-multi-entity-p2p-legacy-approval-system) explains how to build a group-wide approval template that new entities inherit.


## Step 6: Test, Sign Off and Train by Role


User acceptance testing should use real documents from each entity, covering every tax scenario, currency and approval path. Skipping edge cases here is how go-lives fail.


Training should be role-based and short. Requesters learn to raise a PR and check status. Approvers learn to approve from email or mobile. AP learns exception handling. For markets like Thailand and Vietnam, deliver training in the local language. Our article on[multilingual P2P adoption](https://peakflo.co/blog/multilingual-p2p-software-southeast-asia-user-adoption) covers this in detail.


[Prosci’s change management research](https://www.prosci.com/methodology/adkar) consistently shows that projects with structured, role-based change management are far more likely to meet objectives, and that matters most for systems used by non-finance staff.


## Step 7: Rehearse Cutover, Then Go Live


A cutover dry run rehearses go-live while the old process still runs:


- Load open POs and unpaid invoices
- Switch supplier invoice inboxes to the new capture address
- Enable ERP integrations and confirm the first postings
- Confirm SSO access for all users
- Check approval emails reach the right people


Following[PMI guidance on project closure and transition](https://www.pmi.org/learning/library) , after go-live, plan two to four weeks of hypercare with daily check-ins on failed postings, stuck approvals and user questions.


## Step 8: Measure, Learn and Start the Next Batch


Before starting the next batch, compare results against the baseline:


Metric What it shows Review question


Spend through approved PRs Control coverage Is purchasing happening inside the system?


PR-to-PO cycle time Front-end speed Are approvals faster than before?


Invoice touchless rate Capture and matching quality What share of invoices posts without human input?


Exception rate by type Configuration gaps Which tolerances or master data need fixing?


Approval turnaround Approver engagement Are approvers acting from email and mobile?


Active users by market Adoption Are requesters raising their own PRs?


[McKinsey’s research on procurement transformation](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/operations/our-insights) emphasises measuring adoption and compliance alongside efficiency. A system that is fast but bypassed is not a success.


## Budgeting a Multi-Country Rollout


Mid-market P2P platforms usually price on a combination of users and document volume, plus a one-time implementation fee per deployment cycle. When budgeting:


- Ask whether every user needs a licence, including occasional requesters, and whether pricing is flat or tiered by role
- Confirm whether API usage is included or charged separately
- Budget implementation per batch rather than as one figure, since markets are often deployed in separate cycles
- Include internal effort for UAT and training, which is often underestimated


As a broad guide, one-time implementation fees for mid-market P2P projects commonly range from around 10,000 to 50,000 US dollars or more per deployment cycle, depending on integration complexity and number of markets. Licensing models vary widely between vendors, so compare total cost over three years rather than headline per-user prices. The team in our example noted that pricing had already ruled out several vendors on their shortlist.[Gartner’s procurement and finance research](https://www.gartner.com/en/finance) recommends comparing total cost of ownership rather than licence fees alone.

## Our Verdict: Big Bang or Phased?


### Choose a phased rollout if


- You operate in three or more countries
- Markets differ in language, tax or process maturity
- Key users cannot all be available for one UAT window
- You want early results to support later budget approvals


### Consider a single big-bang go-live if


- You have two or fewer entities with identical processes
- All users share a working language and tax regime
- You have a hard deadline, such as legacy system decommissioning, for all markets at once


**Our Recommendation:** For Southeast Asian groups, a phased rollout in two or three batches is almost always the safer choice. Start with the highest-volume, most similar markets, lock down ERP scope and approval design before configuration, and put your final approver in the POC. Each subsequent batch then reuses proven templates and goes faster.


## Conclusion


A multi-country P2P rollout is won or lost in planning. Narrow phase 1 scope, a settled ERP integration decision, data-driven market sequencing and a POC with the real approver are what keep a five-country programme on schedule.


With those in place, each 12 to 16 week cycle becomes repeatable. The first batch proves the design, and the batches that follow reuse it.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a phased P2P rollout?


A phased P2P rollout deploys procure-to-pay software one batch of countries or entities at a time, rather than all at once. Each batch goes through design, configuration, testing, training and go-live, and lessons from earlier batches are applied to later ones.


### Which country should go live first in a Southeast Asian P2P rollout?


Start with the markets that generate the most purchase and invoice transactions relative to their complexity, not necessarily the country with the most staff. High-volume, well-documented markets prove the design under real load and deliver visible savings early.


### How long does a P2P implementation take per market batch?


A typical deployment cycle for a mid-market P2P implementation is 12 to 16 weeks per batch, covering preparation, design, configuration, user acceptance testing, sign-off, role-based training, cutover dry run and go-live.


### Should multiple countries be batched together?


Yes, where they share processes, languages or ERP setup. Batching two similar markets together, such as Malaysia and Singapore, reduces total implementation cycles and cost. Markets with distinct tax or language needs may justify their own batch.


### What should a P2P proof of concept include?


A useful POC runs real purchase requests, purchase orders and supplier invoices from your own entities through the platform, including approval routing, invoice capture in local languages, matching, tax handling and a test ERP posting. The final approver should attend.


### Who should be involved in approving a regional P2P project?


A common structure is a finance analyst who runs discovery and vendor groundwork, a regional finance director who joins for demos and pricing, and a regional VP or CFO who attends the POC and approves the project. IT and the ERP team must confirm integration scope early.


### What usually delays a multi-country P2P rollout?


The most common delays are an undecided ERP integration scope, unclear approval matrices, master data that is not clean, tax scenarios discovered late in testing and key users unavailable during UAT. Most can be avoided by resolving scope and data before configuration starts.


### How much does a multi-country P2P implementation cost?


Costs vary widely by scope. Mid-market P2P platforms typically combine a monthly subscription based on users and document volume with a one-time implementation fee per deployment cycle, which commonly ranges from around 10,000 to 50,000 US dollars or more depending on integration and number of markets.


### What is a cutover dry run?


A cutover dry run rehearses the go-live weekend: loading open POs and unpaid invoices, switching email inboxes, enabling integrations and confirming that the first transactions post correctly. It surfaces issues while the old process is still running.


### How do you measure success after each rollout phase?


Track spend under approved purchase requests, PR-to-PO cycle time, invoice touchless rate, exception rate, approval turnaround and user adoption per market. Compare each batch against its baseline before starting the next one.
